## About Me

<!-- bio:start -->
I study how research evidence is produced, reported and used in public policy. Much of what researchers find is never published, so my main research measures what goes missing. To do that, I take the hypotheses that research teams publicly stated before their study began, write each one down in a common format, and check years later whether its result is available anywhere. I also work on making policy analysis more transparent. By policy analysis I mean the studies that estimate what a proposed policy would cost or do. Those studies should show their assumptions, so that readers can check them and change them. I believe economics is entering a new stage in how evidence is reported and used in policy. I aspire to be part of the group of researchers studying and strengthening the link between evidence and policy.

Most recently, I worked at UC Berkeley as a staff researcher. There I developed a framework for making policy analysis transparent, along with interactive demonstrations that let readers change the assumptions behind a policy estimate and watch the result move. I also co-led a three-year project on missing results in economics. We took over 5,000 hypotheses that research teams had registered in advance and checked how many had a publicly available result 8 to 9 years later. Fewer than half did. We then ran a randomized experiment with those research teams to find out what keeps results from being reported ([my job market paper](https://fhoces.github.io/research.html#job-market-paper)).

Before that, I did my PhD in Public Policy at RAND. My dissertation asked how policy analysis can be made more transparent and easier to reproduce, so that policy rests more firmly on evidence. Before my PhD, I studied economics (BA and master's at U. de Chile, MA at UPenn) and worked in Chile's public sector, measuring the effects of social programs and doing economic analysis of social policies.
<!-- bio:end -->
